findings.title: Billing webhook is outside the authenticated prefix list and verifies no signature, so anyone can change any tenant's plan, seat count and suspension state
findings.class: Missing authentication on a state-changing endpoint
findings.evidence: hooks.server.ts:6 declares PROTECTED_PREFIXES = ['/admin', '/api/reports'] and needsSession (line 9) returns true only for those two prefixes. '/api/internal/webhooks' matches neither, so the 401 at line 20 never fires for it. The handler itself reads request.json() at line 17, checks only that tenant_id and event are present, and then runs UPDATE statements against the tenants table using getDb() — the unscoped handle, which does not go through the tenant pin. There is no HMAC check, no shared-secret header, no timestamp and no replay window anywhere in the file. default_resolver.py flagged hooks.server.ts:9 as a silent fallback on exactly this line.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller who can reach the service sets any tenant's plan and seats (line 29-30), which the file's own comment says the feature flags are derived from, un-suspends a suspended tenant (line 31), or suspends any tenant by posting subscription.cancelled (line 39). Each call also flushes the whole report cache (line 48), which is a free cache-stampede primitive.
findings.recommendation: Verify the provider's signature over the raw body with a constant-time comparison before parsing, reject callbacks outside a short timestamp window, and add the route's prefix to a deny-by-default list so a new route under /api is authenticated unless it is explicitly exempted, rather than unauthenticated unless it is explicitly listed.

triage.reason: The only unskippable layer in front of the handler is the handle hook at hooks.server.ts:12, and its own prefix list excludes this path. No signature verification exists in the file or in $lib/server.
payload.tenant_id, payload.plan and payload.seats come straight from request.json() at line 17 with no allowlist between the parse and the UPDATE.
The path segment 'internal' names an intent, not a control: nothing in the tree binds this route to a private listener, a network policy or an allowlisted source address.

findings.title: Admin form actions suspend tenants and change plans with no authorization of their own; the platform-admin check lives in a layout load that does not run on the action request
findings.evidence: The isPlatformAdmin check is at routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13, inside a LayoutServerLoad. SvelteKit resolves a form-action POST by running the action first and the load functions afterwards to re-render, so the action body at lines 38-43 executes before that load is ever entered. The only thing in front of the action is hooks.server.ts:19, which returns 401 solely when locals.session is absent — it never inspects isPlatformAdmin. Neither action re-checks the role: suspend (line 38) takes no arguments beyond params and writes immediately, and updatePlan (line 23) validates only that the plan string is one of three literals. Both use getDb(), the unscoped handle.
findings.impact: Any authenticated console user, including one with no platform role at all, suspends any tenant by id or moves it between billing plans, and the file's comment at +layout.server.ts:4 states that the suspension switch is precisely what /admin exists to protect. Suspension is a denial of service against a paying tenant; the plan change is a billing and entitlement change.
findings.recommendation: Move the platform-admin assertion into each action body (or into the handle hook keyed on pathname and method), and treat +layout.server.ts as presentation only. A load function is not an authorization boundary for actions in this framework.

triage.reason: The candidate compensating control is routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13. It is not on the action path, and hooks.server.ts:19 — which is on the path — checks only that a session exists. triage.md: a control the caller may forget, or that the framework does not run, is not this rule.
The exposure is not narrower than it reads: the route matcher constrains only the shape of tid, not who may call it, so every tenant id in the database is reachable.
Two principals: an ordinary tenant operator holding a console session, and the platform staff whose tenants they can suspend.

findings.title: Platform-admin status is granted from a request header the application never proves came from the edge proxy
findings.evidence: resolveSession reads headers.get('x-console-role') at line 43 and sets isPlatformAdmin when that string equals 'platform-admin' (line 49). The headers object passed in is event.request.headers — the caller's own headers, forwarded verbatim from hooks.server.ts:16. The comment at lines 12-13 asserts that an edge proxy stamps this header after matching a client certificate, but nothing in the tree strips or overwrites an inbound x-console-role: there is no allowlist of trusted proxy addresses, no shared secret on the header, and no second signal corroborating it. The value is ORed with the JWT claim, so the header alone is sufficient.
findings.impact: Any caller who can reach the origin directly — a misrouted request, a pod-to-pod call, a second ingress, a path that bypasses the proxy — becomes a platform administrator by adding one header, which unlocks the whole /admin surface including tenant suspension and plan changes.
findings.recommendation: Derive isPlatformAdmin only from the verified token claim, or from a server-side lookup keyed on the subject. If a proxy-stamped header must be trusted, terminate it: strip x-console-role from every inbound request at the first hop the application controls, and bind it to a value only the proxy can produce.

triage.reason: No stripping layer exists in the repository. hooks.server.ts is the first application code to see the request and it passes headers through untouched at line 16.

The edge proxy configuration is not in the tree and no exported artifact was provided, so I cannot establish that it strips the header. triage.md is explicit that without the artifact this is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS. Status is nevertheless confirmed on the second, independent leg: the header is ORed with the claim, so even a correct proxy leaves the OR in place for any request that does not traverse it.
The value's origin is a request header, which is attacker-controlled by definition unless a hop rewrites it.

findings.title: JWT verification checks the HMAC but never the expiry, issuer or audience, so a leaked console token is valid forever
findings.evidence: verifyJwt splits the token, recomputes HMAC-SHA256 over head.body and compares with timingSafeEqual (lines 20-26). It returns a boolean and reads no claim. decodeClaims (line 32) then parses the payload and resolveSession consumes sub, tid, email and role — but nothing anywhere in the file or in hooks.server.ts reads exp, nbf, iat, iss or aud. grep over the tree returns no occurrence of 'exp' as a claim check. There is also no revocation list and no server-side session record to invalidate.
findings.impact: A token captured from a log, a browser history entry, a shared machine or a proxy cache authenticates indefinitely, and signing out cannot revoke it because there is no server-side state. A token minted for one environment or audience is accepted by any deployment sharing CONSOLE_JWT_SECRET.
findings.recommendation: Validate exp (and nbf where present) inside verifyJwt before returning true, pin iss and aud to expected values, and keep a server-side session or revocation list so a sign-out or a compromise can be acted on.

triage.reason: The hook at hooks.server.ts:15 calls verifyJwt and nothing else; there is no session store lookup that would bound the token's life independently.
The sink is an access decision: resolveSession's output populates locals.session, which gates /admin and /api/reports.

This is not the alg-confusion variant — the verifier fixes HS256 and ignores the token header, which is correct. The defect is the absent lifetime and audience checks, which is a separate half of WEB-01.

findings.title: Report cache key is the report slug and the window, with no tenant component, so one tenant's report body is served to every other tenant
findings.class: Cross-tenant data exposure through a shared cache key
findings.evidence: reportKey at lib/server/cache.ts:20 returns `report:v3:${reportId}:${range}` — no tenant. The handler builds that key at line 22 and returns the cached body at line 24 before any tenant-scoped query is issued (getTenantDb is only reached at line 26, on a miss). The comment at lines 15-16 states that params.id is a shared template slug, so every tenant that installed a template addresses the identical key. The cached object is not a summary: it carries generatedFor (the producing tenant id) and the full rows — bucket, gross_cents, net_cents, currency and counterparty (line 28) — and is written with a one-hour TTL at line 43.
findings.impact: The first tenant to request a given template and window populates the cache; for the next hour every other tenant requesting the same slug receives that tenant's revenue rows and counterparty names, and can read the producing tenant's id out of generatedFor. No exploitation is needed beyond calling the endpoint with a common slug.
findings.recommendation: Include the tenant id in the cache key — `report:v4:${tenantId}:${reportId}:${range}` — and assert on read that the cached body's generatedFor matches the caller's tenant before returning it. Bump the version segment so existing poisoned entries are abandoned.

triage.reason: The cache read at line 23 precedes every scoping mechanism in the request: the session is only used later, at line 26, and the row-level policy never runs on a cache hit.
The cached rows are settlement and chargeback figures with counterparty names — financial records belonging to a specific tenant, not public content.
The key is as wide as it reads and nothing narrows it: reportKey has exactly two inputs and both are caller-supplied.

findings.title: The tenant scoping handle sets a transaction-local variable outside a transaction and returns the shared pool, so the row-level-security pin the report queries rely on is not in effect
findings.class: Security control that does not do what it declares
findings.evidence: getTenantDb issues `select set_config('app.tenant_id', ${tenantId}, true)` as a standalone tagged-template query on the pool and then returns the pool itself (line 17). Two independent defects: the third argument true makes the setting transaction-local, and a lone statement is its own implicit transaction, so the value is discarded the moment that statement completes; and the returned handle is the pool, not the connection the set_config ran on, so the caller's next query may be dispatched to a different connection. The doc comment at lines 11-14 asserts the opposite — 'a query that forgets its WHERE clause still comes back scoped' — and the two consumers take it at its word: routes/api/reports/+server.ts:67 selects from reports with no tenant predicate at all, and routes/api/reports/[id]/+server.ts:27 filters only on report_slug and window.
findings.impact: If the row-level policy is permissive when app.tenant_id is unset, both report endpoints return every tenant's rows to any authenticated caller. If it is restrictive, the endpoints return nothing and the feature is broken. Either way the control that the two callers depend on is inert, and the comment makes it look present — which is the expensive half of this class, because it is what a reviewer answers FP-01 with.
findings.recommendation: Reserve a connection and run the pin and the query inside one transaction — postgres.js `pool.begin(async sql => { await sql\`select set_config('app.tenant_id', ${tenantId}, false)\`; ... })` — or drop the pin entirely and put an explicit tenant_id predicate on every statement. Add a negative test that asserts a query issued through getTenantDb for tenant A cannot see a row belonging to tenant B.

triage.reason: This function is itself the claimed compensating control; there is no second one. The two callers carry no tenant predicate of their own (reports/+server.ts:67 has no WHERE clause).

The row-level-security policy lives in the database and no schema or migration is in the tree, so I cannot establish whether an unset app.tenant_id fails open or closed. Per triage.md this caps the finding at probable; the defect in the application code is confirmed regardless of which way the policy falls.
There is no reading under which set_config(..., true) on a pooled tagged-template call survives past its own statement.

findings.title: The report digest escapes the title and the owner and interpolates the notes field raw into the HTML fragment
findings.evidence:
digest builds an HTML list at lines 48-54. row.title and row.owner both go through escapeHtml (line 51); row.notes on line 52 is interpolated directly into `

${row.notes}

`. escapeHtml exists eight lines above and covers &, <, >, " and '. The fragment is returned with content-type text/html at line 76 when ?format=html is set, and the comment at lines 45-46 states it is piped straight into a mail template. The asymmetry within one template literal is the evidence that the author regarded these values as untrusted.
findings.impact: A notes value containing markup executes in whatever renders the digest — the browser of anyone who fetches ?format=html, and, since the fragment is piped into the weekly mail template, any HTML mail client that does not sanitise. Because notes is stored, the payload persists and fires for every subsequent render.
findings.recommendation: Wrap row.notes in escapeHtml like its two siblings, and add a test that renders a row whose fields all contain angle brackets and asserts the output has none unescaped.

triage.reason: No writer for reports.notes exists in the tree — the table is only ever read (reports/+server.ts:68) — so I cannot trace the value back to a request. Its two siblings in the same row are escaped, which is evidence the author expected external input, but I cannot prove it. Per triage.md this caps the finding at probable.
No sanitiser sits between the query at line 67 and the interpolation at line 52, and hooks.server.ts sets no Content-Security-Policy — only x-content-type-options and referrer-policy (lines 36-37).
The response is served as text/html; charset=utf-8 at line 76, so the sink interprets markup.

findings.title: Authentication is skipped for any path containing the substring /health, which exempts the device heartbeat route and lets an unauthenticated caller re-pin any device's firmware channel
findings.class: Authentication bypass through a substring path match
findings.evidence: skipsAuth returns true when strings.Contains(path, "/health") — a substring test, not a prefix or an equality. router.go:35 registers POST /v1/devices/:id/health-report on the authenticated group, and that path contains "/health", so RequireFleetToken returns at line 28 without ever reading the Authorization header. The handler it releases, HealthReport at handlers/devices.go:102, writes twice: RecordHeartbeat (store/devices.go:127) and, whenever the body carries a non-empty firmware_channel, SetFirmwareChannel (store/devices.go:136), whose statement filters on the device id alone with no tenant and no serial.
findings.impact: With no credential at all, a caller who knows or guesses a device UUID sets that device's firmware_channel to any string, across tenants. The comment at handlers/devices.go:99-101 states this is how a site converges onto a channel without an operator, so the effect is that the next provisioning cycle pulls whatever image sits in the attacker-named channel — and the firmware upload endpoint that fills those channels is itself unauthenticated (reported separately). It also lets an unauthenticated caller falsify heartbeat, uptime and battery telemetry, which drives the NOC's online and degraded counters.
findings.recommendation: Replace the substring test with an exact allowlist of the two paths that are genuinely public — "/healthz" and "/metrics" — matched by equality, and move the heartbeat route back behind the token. If per-device credentials are needed for gateways, issue them; a path spelling is not a credential.

triage.reason: The middleware chain in front is gin.Recovery, RequestLog, CanonicalPath and PerClientRate (router.go:15-16); none of them authenticates. RequireFleetToken is the only authenticator and it is the one that returns early.
The narrowing runs the wrong way: the construct reads as an exemption for health probes and in fact applies to a state-changing device route as well. That is wider than it looks, not narrower.
The comment justifies exempting liveness probes from a token lookup, which is bounded; exempting a route that writes to the devices table is not what that justification covers.

findings.title: The firmware group is registered without the token middleware, leaving unauthenticated download and unauthenticated upload of gateway images
findings.class: Missing authentication on a sibling route group
findings.evidence: Line 30 creates the API group with the guard: `api := r.Group("/v1", middleware.RequireFleetToken(deps.Store))`. Line 43 creates a second group from the engine, not from that group: `fw := r.Group("/v1/firmware")`, with no middleware argument and no fw.Use anywhere. gin attaches group middleware to the routes registered on that group object only, so GET and PUT /v1/firmware/:channel/:file (lines 44-45) inherit nothing but the four global middlewares at lines 15-16, none of which authenticates. UploadFirmware (handlers/firmware.go:37) then creates the channel directory if it does not exist and writes the request body to the named file with O_TRUNC, checking nothing about the caller, the content or a signature.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the port replaces or introduces a firmware image in any channel, and the comment at handlers/firmware.go:36 says a provisioning rsync job then distributes it to gateways. That is remote code execution on the fleet by way of an unauthenticated HTTP PUT. The same group also serves every image for download, and O_TRUNC means an attacker can silently truncate a legitimate release.
findings.recommendation: Register the firmware routes on the guarded group (or pass middleware.RequireFleetToken to r.Group at line 43), require a release-engineering role for PUT specifically, and verify a detached signature over the image before it is written into a channel the provisioning job reads.

triage.reason: The global middlewares are Recovery, RequestLog, CanonicalPath and PerClientRate. CanonicalPath rejects dot segments and PerClientRate shapes traffic; neither establishes identity.

The comment at lines 40-42 argues the images are pulled over a provisioning VLAN, but nothing in the tree binds this group to a separate listener or interface: main.go:46 serves every route on the single cfg.Listen address.
Two principals: release engineering, which is meant to promote builds, and everyone else who can reach the port.

findings.title: An unrecognised bearer token authenticates successfully as the baseline operator role instead of being rejected
findings.evidence: RoleForToken hashes the presented token and looks it up in token_roles. On sql.ErrNoRows — that is, when the token is unknown — it returns Principal{Role: baselineRole} and a nil error (line 59), where baselineRole is "operator" (line 46). middleware/auth.go rejects only two things: an empty Authorization header (line 33) and a lookup that returns an error (line 39), and then rejects an empty role (line 42). A baseline principal has a non-empty role, so it passes at line 49 and the request proceeds with CtxRole=operator and CtxTenantID empty.
findings.impact: The bearer token is not a credential: any non-empty string authenticates. That defeats revocation entirely — deleting a token's row in token_roles promotes it to the baseline role rather than disabling it — and it means every rate limit, audit line and role check downstream is anchored on an identity nobody proved. The tenant lands empty, so tenant-filtered reads return nothing, but writes that do not filter on tenant still land: EnqueueCommand inserts a row (store/devices.go:183) and the heartbeat route writes device state with no tenant predicate at all.
findings.recommendation: Return an explicit not-found from RoleForToken on ErrNoRows and have the middleware reject it with 401. If pre-role gateways genuinely need to keep working, enumerate them: give them rows in token_roles carrying the baseline role, so the fallback is a list of known principals rather than the absence of one.

triage.reason: The middleware is the only authenticator and it treats the fallback principal as valid at auth.go:42-49. No later layer re-checks the token.

The comment at lines 42-45 bounds the intent to legacy gateways with no role row, but the implementation is unbounded: it applies to every token the table does not contain, including one an attacker invents.
Nothing narrows the branch — there is no device-id check, no issued-before date, no allowlist. It is exactly as wide as it reads.

findings.title: Heartbeat and firmware-channel writes carry no tenant predicate, so an operator of one tenant can write to another tenant's devices
findings.class: BOLA / missing tenant scoping on write
findings.evidence: Every read path in this store filters on tenant: ListDevices (line 95), GetDevice (line 82) and FailedCommands (line 214) all bind tenant_id. The two write paths reached from HealthReport do not. SetFirmwareChannel's statement is `update devices set firmware_channel = $2 ... where id = $1` — id alone. RecordHeartbeat (line 130) filters on id and serial, both supplied by the same request (handlers/devices.go:110 passes c.Param("id") and rep.Serial), so it is self-certifying rather than scoped. Neither handler consults middleware.CtxTenantID, and HealthReport is the one handler in devices.go that never mentions it.
findings.impact: Given a device UUID, the holder of any token — or, through the /health substring exemption reported separately, no token — rewrites that device's firmware channel and its telemetry regardless of which tenant owns it. Device UUIDs leak through the wallboard refresh loop and through command responses, so they are not a secret.
findings.recommendation: Add `and tenant_id = $n` to both statements and pass middleware.CtxTenantID from HealthReport, matching what ListDevices and GetDevice already do. Assert the affected-row count and return 404 when it is zero.

triage.reason: There is no ORM-level tenant scope in this codebase — every statement is hand-written SQL and the scoping is per-statement, which is exactly why the two that omit it are defects.
The serial column in RecordHeartbeat looks like a narrowing condition but is supplied by the same caller in the same body, so it constrains nothing an attacker does not control.
The devices table is explicitly multi-tenant — tenant_id is a column and every other statement filters on it.

findings.title: The retry sweep re-queues stored commands through a writer that applies neither the command allowlist nor the fleet-admin check
findings.class: Authorization gate enforced by one writer and not its sibling
findings.evidence: EnqueueCommand gates every insert twice: allowedCommands at line 38 and adminOnlyCommands versus the caller's role at line 44. RetryFailed, on the same handler type and the same commands table, gates nothing — it has no role check of its own, and the insert it drives, Store.EnqueueRaw (store/devices.go:196), takes the name straight off the stored row and writes it back with no allowlist. The comment at lines 80-82 argues the rows already passed EnqueueCommand on the way in, which is true of the allowlist but not of the role: the role was checked against whoever enqueued the command originally, not against whoever is calling retry now.
findings.impact: An operator calls POST /v1/commands/retry and re-queues any timed-out collect-logs command that a fleet-admin in the same tenant raised earlier — the one command class the code marks as elevated, described at lines 21-22 as shipping the device's rolling buffer back. The role boundary between operator and fleet-admin is bypassed by replay. RetryFailed also carries no per-caller limit, so the same rows can be re-queued repeatedly.
findings.recommendation: Re-apply both checks inside the retry loop: skip a row whose name is not in allowedCommands, and skip a row in adminOnlyCommands unless the caller holds fleet-admin. Better, move both checks into a single admission function that EnqueueCommand and EnqueueRaw share, so a third writer cannot be added without them.

triage.reason: No layer between the router and the store re-checks the command name or the role: router.go:37 registers RetryFailed with only RequireFleetToken in front, which establishes a role but does not compare it to anything.
The two handlers reach the same effect — a row in commands with state 'queued' and a fresh dispatch token — which is the test WEB-24 sets for whether an asymmetry counts.

FailedCommands does scope to the caller's tenant (store/devices.go:214), which narrows the blast radius to one tenant, but the defect is the crossing of a role boundary inside that tenant, which the tenant filter does not touch.

findings.title: The idempotency cache is a process-global map keyed only on a caller-chosen header, so it replays another tenant's command id, device serial and dispatch token
findings.class: Cross-tenant data exposure through a shared cache key
findings.evidence: The map is `idem map[string]json.RawMessage` on the Store (line 21), keyed at RememberIdempotent (line 245) on nothing but the key string. handlers/commands.go:49 takes that key verbatim from the Idempotency-Key request header and, on a hit, returns the stored body with 200 before any tenant, role or device check runs (lines 50-55). The body it returns was built at lines 67-71 and contains command_id, device_serial and dispatch_token. The map has no eviction: nothing deletes from it and no TTL is recorded.
findings.impact: Two tenants using the same idempotency key value — a counter, a date, a shared client library's default — read each other's responses, which discloses device serials and, worse, the dispatch_token minted for that command. An attacker does not need a collision to happen naturally: they can iterate plausible key values and read back whatever is cached. Separately, the unbounded map is a memory-exhaustion primitive, since every distinct key an attacker sends is retained for the process's lifetime.
findings.recommendation: Key the cache on the tuple (tenant id, idempotency key) and verify the tenant on read, not just the key. Give entries a TTL bounded by the command window and evict on expiry, or move the cache to the database with a unique constraint on (tenant_id, key).

triage.reason: The cache hit at commands.go:52 returns before Store.EnqueueCommand is called, so the tenant binding at line 59 is never reached on that path.
dispatch_token is a per-command capability the relay mints from crypto/rand (store/devices.go:170-180) precisely so it is unguessable; handing it to another tenant defeats its purpose.
The key is the Idempotency-Key header, chosen freely by the caller with no format, length or namespace constraint.

findings.title: Outbound TLS verification is disabled by default because the insecure flag is derived from an environment name that falls back to staging
findings.evidence: env comes from getenv("FLEET_ENV", "staging") at line 22, and AllowInsecureTLS is set to `env != "prod"` at line 30. The default therefore evaluates to true. main.go:37 feeds it straight into `&tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: cfg.AllowInsecureTLS}` on the callbacks client, which main.go:32-33 describes as the leg the relay uses to call back into each site's device gateway. Nothing else validates the peer: there is no custom VerifyPeerCertificate, no pinned RootCAs, no certificate allowlist. The default database URL on line 27 carries sslmode=disable for the same reason.
findings.impact: Unless an operator remembers to set FLEET_ENV=prod exactly, every production deployment accepts any certificate on its outbound callbacks — including a self-signed one from an attacker on the path — so command confirmations, and the dispatch tokens they carry, can be intercepted and forged. The failure mode is silent: nothing logs or refuses to start when a production deployment runs with the staging default.
findings.recommendation: Invert the default so verification is on unless an environment explicitly opts out (`AllowInsecureTLS: env == "lab"` or a dedicated FLEET_ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS flag that defaults to false), and load the internal CA into the transport's RootCAs so the lab gateways can be verified rather than skipped. Log loudly at start-up whenever verification is off.

triage.reason: This is not a development-only path removed by the build: the flag is read at run time from the process environment (config.go:22), so the insecure branch ships in the same binary as the secure one and is selected by an absent variable.
No mutual-TLS, no request signing and no allowlist compensates on the outbound leg; main.go:34-41 constructs the client with a timeout and connection limits only.

Nothing narrows the expression: env != "prod" is evaluated once at start-up over the whole process and feeds the single callbacks transport at main.go:37, so it applies to every outbound request the relay makes. Setting FLEET_ENV is an input to the defective expression, not a control in another layer, which is why FP-08 is not the rule this class turns on.

findings.title: The rate limiter is keyed on a client address the caller can set, and its bucket map has an eviction field that nothing reads
findings.class: Rate limiting that can be evaded, plus unbounded resource growth
findings.evidence: The key is c.ClientIP() (line 32). gin resolves that from X-Forwarded-For and X-Real-IP whenever the remote address is a trusted proxy, and the engine here is built with gin.New() at router.go:14 with no SetTrustedProxies call anywhere in the tree, which leaves gin's default of trusting all proxies. Separately, bucket carries a `seen time.Time` field (line 17) written on every request at line 40; grep over the whole tree returns that assignment and the struct field and no reader — there is no sweep goroutine, no expiry check and no delete from the buckets map (line 22).
findings.impact: A caller rotates the X-Forwarded-For header per request and never trips the limit, which removes the only brake in front of the unauthenticated firmware upload and the unauthenticated heartbeat route. The same rotation grows the buckets map without bound: one *rate.Limiter plus a map entry per forged address, retained for the process's lifetime, which is a memory-exhaustion path that needs no credential. The declared knob FLEET_RATE_BURST is real and read, but what it bounds is per-key, and the key is free.
findings.recommendation: Call r.SetTrustedProxies with the actual ingress addresses (or an empty list, which makes ClientIP fall back to the socket address) so the key cannot be spoofed; key on the authenticated principal in addition to the address for routes that have one; and either sweep the map using the seen field that already exists or replace it with an LRU with a hard capacity.

triage.reason: PerClientRate is the only limiter in the tree; the header is not normalised anywhere before it, since CanonicalPath (middleware/auth.go:55) inspects only the path.

An upstream load balancer might overwrite X-Forwarded-For, which would fix the spoofing half. No configuration for one was provided, so this is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS — and it would not touch the unbounded-map half, which is why the finding stays confirmed.
This is not defence in depth behind a working control: it is the only rate control, and it stands in front of routes that need no credential at all.

findings.title: The request logger writes the decoded request path into a line-oriented log with no neutralisation, so a caller can forge log records
findings.evidence: log.Printf("%s %s %d %s", c.Request.Method, c.Request.URL.Path, c.Writer.Status(), ...) writes URL.Path into Go's standard logger, which is one record per line. Go's net/http percent-decodes the request target into URL.Path before any handler sees it, so a target containing %0A arrives as a literal newline in that string. Nothing escapes it: CanonicalPath (middleware/auth.go:57) rejects only "..", and there is no structured encoder — router.go:15 registers this middleware directly. It runs before authentication (RequireFleetToken is attached per-group at router.go:30), so the value is unauthenticated-caller-controlled.
findings.impact: One request writes two or more records. An attacker appends a fabricated line — a successful authentication, a different status code, a different source — into the same stream the operators and any downstream line-based aggregator read, which destroys the accountability of the log at precisely the moment it matters. If the log is ever rendered in a viewer as HTML, the same input becomes stored cross-site scripting reached without touching the application.
findings.recommendation: Emit structured records (one JSON object per event, with the path as a field) or escape control characters — strconv.Quote on the path is a one-line fix — and confirm the consumer parses the structured format rather than splitting on newlines.

triage.reason: URL.Path is the request target, chosen by the caller. No allowlist or pattern constrains it before line 55: the only path inspection in the tree is the ".." substring test.
The sink is text/line-oriented — the log package writes one newline-terminated record per call — which is exactly the format in which a newline forges a record.
Unlike the equivalent line in session-broker, which logs a WHATWG URL pathname that keeps %0A encoded, Go decodes the path first. The two look identical and only one is a defect; this is the one.

findings.title: The public-prefix exemption is a startsWith test, so /api/grants/publications is treated as public and returns embargoed grants to unauthenticated callers
findings.class: Authorization bypass through an unanchored prefix match
findings.evidence: PUBLIC_PREFIXES contains "/api/grants/public" (line 30) and line 46 exempts any request whose path startsWith one of them, returning before the OPA call. GrantResource declares @Path("publications") at line 79 under the class-level @Path("/api/grants"), so its full path is "/api/grants/publications" — which startsWith "/api/grants/public" is true for. The intended public route is publicRegister at line 87, @Path("public/register"), and it deliberately calls publications(false). The exempted endpoint instead defaults includeEmbargoed to true (@DefaultValue("true"), line 81), which selects the branch at GrantRepository.java:43 with no embargo predicate, and the comment at lines 74-77 says these rows carry the internal award notes comms stages ahead of an announcement.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller issues GET /api/grants/publications and receives every approved grant including the embargoed ones — reference, title, amount, department and status for up to 1000 rows — before any announcement. The intended public register, one path segment away, correctly excludes them, which is what makes this a bypass rather than a design choice.
findings.recommendation: Match the exemption on a path segment boundary — compare against "/api/grants/public/" with the trailing separator, or test equality against an explicit list of public paths — and flip the includeEmbargoed default to false so the safe value is the one a caller gets by saying nothing.

triage.reason: AuthzFilter is the only authorization layer on this resource and it is the one returning early at line 47. There is no @RolesAllowed, no @PreAuthorize and no service-layer check: GrantResource.publications (line 80) calls the repository directly.
This is the opposite of FP-11: the construct reads narrower than it applies. 'PUBLIC_PREFIXES' promises three named public areas and in fact opens a fourth endpoint nobody listed.
The embargoed rows are by definition not yet public — the embargoedUntil column and the separate public register exist precisely to keep them back.

findings.title: AttachmentResource carries no @Authorized annotation, so the whole attachment surface runs with no authorization decision at all
findings.class: Missing function-level authorization on a whole resource
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter is a @Provider bound with @Authorized (AuthzFilter.java:17-18), and @Authorized is a @NameBinding annotation (Authorized.java:14). A name-bound filter runs only on resources or methods carrying the annotation. GrantResource declares it at GrantResource.java:28; AttachmentResource does not — its declaration at lines 31-33 is @Path, @Produces and nothing else. The two methods it exposes, download (line 44) and ingestManifest (line 65), therefore reach their bodies with no decision from the policy sidecar, and neither performs a check of its own: download resolves the file straight from the grant id in the path, and no code compares that grant against the caller.
findings.impact: Any caller who can reach the service downloads any grant's attachments by iterating the numeric grantId — the signed award letter and the due diligence pack, per the class comment at lines 27-30 — and posts manifests against any grant. The asymmetry with GrantResource, which is annotated, is what establishes that this is an omission rather than a design decision.
findings.recommendation: Annotate the class with @Authorized, and change the default so the filter is not name-bound at all: make it a global ContainerRequestFilter with an explicit, equality-matched allowlist of public paths, so a new resource is protected unless someone exempts it rather than exposed unless someone remembers.

triage.reason: The claimed compensating layer is AuthzFilter, and @NameBinding is precisely the mechanism that prevents it from running here. No web.xml, no security constraint and no @RolesAllowed exists in the tree.
The two resources reach comparable effects on the same grant records and one is annotated while the other is not — the WEB-24 asymmetry test, decidable by comparing two class declarations.
Grants belong to departments and the policy at authz.rego:11 keys entitlements on the caller's department, so there are plainly multiple principals with different rights over these records.

findings.title: The manifest parser builds a DocumentBuilderFactory with external entity resolution and DTD processing left at their defaults (XXE)
findings.evidence: Lines 66-72 create the factory, set namespaceAware, ignoringComments and coalescing, and then parse the request body. The three features that matter are absent: no setFeature(XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, true), no "http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", no setXIncludeAware(false) and no setExpandEntityReferences(false), and no EntityResolver is installed on the builder. The JDK default for DocumentBuilderFactory resolves external entities, and the method consumes an untrusted body: it is @Consumes(APPLICATION_XML) taking the raw InputStream (line 65), reachable — per the previous finding — with no authorization at all.
findings.impact: A posted manifest containing a DOCTYPE with a SYSTEM entity makes the service read local files (the datasource credentials in application.properties, container secrets, /proc) and issue requests from its own network position to the OPA sidecar on loopback and to anything else inside the pod network, which is server-side request forgery from a trusted origin. Parameter-entity variants also give a straightforward denial of service.
findings.recommendation: Disable DTDs outright before parsing — factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true) plus FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING and setXIncludeAware(false) — or, since the manifest is a flat list of file elements, parse it with a streaming reader configured with IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false and SUPPORT_DTD=false.

triage.reason: Nothing pre-validates the body: it goes from the JAX-RS InputStream at line 65 into builder.parse at line 72 with no schema check, size cap beyond the 32M HTTP limit, or content inspection. The 32M limit does not constrain entity expansion.
The parsed document is the request body. The class comment describes an exporter as the intended producer, but nothing authenticates that producer — see the missing @Authorized on the same class.

The sink is a DOM parser with entity resolution enabled, which is the interpreting form of the sink. sanitize() at line 87 runs on the extracted attribute values, long after the entity has already been resolved during parse.

findings.title: Authorization fails open: the policy sidecar's error mode is configured to permit, so every request is allowed whenever the sidecar is slow or restarting
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter declares @ConfigProperty(name = "grants.authz.on-error", defaultValue = "deny") at line 39 — the code's own default is correct. application.properties:15 overrides it with permit. The catch block at lines 55-58 turns any exception from opa.evaluate into Decision.onError(onError), and OpaClient.Decision.onError (line 48) returns new Decision(true, ...) when the mode is permit. The window is not hypothetical and not rare: grants.opa.timeout is PT0.4S (line 10) with a 300 ms connect timeout (OpaClient.java:44), and the comment at lines 12-14 says the sidecar is restarted on every bundle publish.
findings.impact: During any sidecar restart, GC pause or 400 ms latency spike, every @Authorized endpoint allows every request — creating, updating and approving grants, and reading the full register — for any caller who reaches the service. An attacker who can add load to the pod, or who simply retries during a bundle roll, chooses when that window opens.
findings.recommendation: Set grants.authz.on-error=deny and fix the availability problem where it lives: cache the last-known-good decision or the bundle locally, raise the timeout, and roll the sidecar without dropping in-flight decisions. If a permit window is genuinely required it must be bounded and loud — a short, rate-limited, alerting break-glass, not a static property.

triage.reason: The filter is the whole authorization layer for annotated resources; when its decision is synthesised as allow there is nothing behind it. GrantResource carries no method-level role check.
This is the production properties file on the main resources path, not a test or dev profile — there is no %dev or %test prefix on the key and no other profile file in the tree.
It is load-bearing rather than defence in depth: the impact is a complete authorization bypass during the window, not a reduced safety margin.

findings.title: A department with no entry in the entitlement matrix falls back to a baseline that grants read, write, approve and export
findings.evidence: entitlements := object.get(data.roles, input.user.dept, data.roles.baseline) — the third argument is the value returned when the key is missing. roles.json:5 gives baseline the grants ["read", "write", "approve", "export"], which is a strict superset of every named department: programmes lacks export, finance and legal have only read and export, comms and it have only read. The lookup key is input.user.dept, which OpaClient.inputFor sets from identity.getAttribute("dept") at OpaClient.java:82 — a nullable attribute that is inserted into the map with no null check and no default, so a principal carrying no dept attribute lands on the same fallback.
findings.impact: Being unknown to the matrix is the most privileged state in the system. A user in a department the bundle has not been rebuilt for, one whose identity provider does not populate the attribute, or one whose dept is misspelled, receives write, approve and export over grant records — including the approve action that the department-based rule is otherwise the only way to reach for a non-approver. The comment at lines 8-10 frames this as a first-day convenience; what it implements is a privilege ceiling for the least-known callers.
findings.recommendation: Make the fallback the least-privileged value, not the most: object.get(data.roles, input.user.dept, {"grants": []}), and give new cost centres an explicit read-only entry. Reject a decision whose input.user.dept is null or empty before the lookup, rather than letting the missing key select the default.

triage.reason: There is no layer behind the policy: AuthzFilter acts solely on decision.allow (AuthzFilter.java:60) and the resource methods perform no further check.

Nothing narrows the fallback — no condition on the action, the resource path or the roles list restricts it, so it applies to every action the baseline names, on every resource, for every unknown department.
input.user.dept comes from the identity's attributes rather than from a literal or an allowlist, and the branch is selected by the value being absent, which needs no attacker control at all.

findings.title: The approval rule is an alternative to the department entitlement rather than an additional requirement, so the workflow role is neither necessary nor sufficient as documented
findings.evidence: The comment at line 26 states 'Approvals need the workflow role on top of the department entitlement.' In Rego, multiple rules with the same name are disjunctive: the body at lines 28-30 makes allow true whenever the action is approve and the caller holds grants.approver, independently of the entitlement rule at lines 13-16. The two are ORed, not ANDed. Since programmes and baseline both list approve among their grants (roles.json:9 and :5), the entitlement rule alone already allows approval, and the approver rule alone already allows it for any department including comms and it, which grant read only.
findings.impact: Two gaps in opposite directions. A user in the programmes department, or in any department the matrix does not know, approves grants without ever holding the grants.approver workflow role — so the segregation of duty the role was introduced to enforce does not exist. And a user holding grants.approver approves grants for a department whose entitlements do not include approval. Approval is the state change that releases money.
findings.recommendation: Express the conjunction explicitly in one rule: `allow if { input.action == "approve"; "grants.approver" in input.user.roles; "approve" in entitlements.grants }`, and remove approve from the baseline grants so an unknown department cannot satisfy the entitlement half.

triage.reason: There is no reading of Rego under which two same-named allow rules conjoin. The construct is exactly what it looks like to a Rego reader and exactly not what the comment beside it claims.
GrantResource.approve (line 69) calls repo.approve directly with no second check, so the policy decision is the only gate on the transition to APPROVED.
This is not an absent extra layer: the rule is the segregation-of-duty control itself, and it does not hold in either direction.

findings.title: The Kafka consumer writes grant amount, department and status with none of the validation the REST endpoint applies to the same fields
findings.class: Validation gate enforced by one writer and not its sibling
findings.evidence: The REST writer constrains every field: GrantPayload (GrantResource.java:36-42) declares @Size(max=240) on title, @DecimalMin("0.00") and @DecimalMax("5000000.00") on amount, @Size(max=32) on dept and @Pattern(regexp="DRAFT|SUBMITTED|APPROVED|REJECTED") on status, and create/update are annotated @Valid. The consumer reads the same record shape off the topic — the class comment at lines 13-17 says so explicitly — and passes it through unchecked: getString("amount", "0") into a raw BigDecimal, getString("dept", "programmes") and getString("status", "DRAFT") straight into repo.applyEvent (lines 43-47), which issues the update with those values bound. The only check is that reference is non-blank (line 38). application.properties declares the five mp.messaging.incoming.grant-events keys with no security.protocol, sasl or ssl setting.
findings.impact: A producer on grants.events.v2 sets a grant's status to a value outside the four-state enum, its amount above the five-million ceiling or negative, and — the sharpest consequence — its dept to a string the entitlement matrix does not contain, which promotes every caller in that department to the baseline grants of read, write, approve and export by way of the fallback reported above. A malformed amount also raises NumberFormatException inside a @Transactional @Incoming method, which halts the consumer on a poison message.
findings.recommendation: Validate the event against the same constraints before it reaches the repository — construct a GrantPayload and run the Validator programmatically, or move the constraints onto the entity — and route rejected messages to a dead-letter topic rather than letting an exception stall the consumer.

triage.reason: No layer between the deserializer and the update applies the constraints: the connector is configured with JsonObjectDeserializer (application.properties:27), which produces an untyped JsonObject, and applyEvent (GrantRepository.java:89) binds the values as given.

Whether the broker restricts who may produce to grants.events.v2 cannot be established: the client properties declare no security protocol or SASL mechanism, and no broker ACL export was provided. Per triage.md that is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS, which caps this finding at probable.
The two writers reach the same effect on the same rows — the REST update and applyEvent both issue an update on GrantEntity setting amount, dept and status — which is the WEB-24 test.

findings.title: A legacy alias route reaches the admin adjustments controller on a path the admin gate does not match, so any partner posts money adjustments
findings.evidence: The admin gate is path-based: ApplicationController runs require_admin only when admin_area? is true (line 8), and admin_area? is request.path.start_with?("/api/v1/admin") (line 29). The canonical route at routes.rb:23 produces /api/v1/admin/adjustments and is covered. The alias at routes.rb:30 dispatches to the same controller action — "admin/adjustments#create" — on the path /api/v1/invoices/:invoice_id/adjust, which does not start with the admin prefix, so require_admin never runs. The comment at lines 26-29 states plainly that it is the same controller and the same payload shape, which is what makes the divergence in enforcement a defect rather than two different features.
findings.impact: Any authenticated partner, with no admin role, posts an adjustment against an invoice and drives LedgerPosting#credit! (adjustments_controller.rb:31), which the controller comment at lines 17-19 describes as the one place a partner can move money that has already been posted. The gate that exists for exactly this action is bypassed by using the older URL.
findings.recommendation: Anchor authorization on the controller rather than on the request path: put `before_action :require_admin` in Admin::AdjustmentsController (or in an Admin::BaseController it inherits from) so every route that reaches the action is covered, and keep admin_area? only as a coarse second layer. Then retire the alias.

triage.reason: The only filters that run are authenticate_partner! and coerce_pagination (application_controller.rb:6-7). The controller declares no authorization of its own and no Pundit/CanCan policy exists in the tree.
Both routes reach the identical action with the identical params contract; the routes file says so in its own comment.
The alias is not narrower: it accepts invoice_id from the path (adjustments_controller.rb:39 prefers params[:invoice_id]), so it reaches at least as many invoices as the canonical route.

findings.title: Adjustment creation resolves the invoice with an unscoped find, so a partner posts credits against another organisation's invoices
findings.evidence: ApplicationController provides scoped_invoices (line 46) as Invoice.where(org_id: current_user.org_id) and the comment above it at line 45 claims every read and write goes through the caller's organisation. index in this same controller honours that, joining invoices and filtering on invoices: { org_id: current_user.org_id } (line 8). create does not: line 21 is Invoice.find(invoice_id) against the global scope, and invoice_id (line 38) is taken from params with no ownership test. The invoice then flows into Adjustment.create! and into LedgerPosting#credit! (line 31) unchecked.
findings.impact: A partner supplies any invoice id and posts a credit against it, reducing another organisation's invoice amount and writing a LedgerEntry attributed to their own user. The neighbouring index action proves the scope was available and was simply not used on the write path.
findings.recommendation: Change line 21 to scoped_invoices.find(invoice_id); the existing rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound (line 10) then turns a cross-org attempt into a 404 with no extra code. Add a request spec with two organisations that asserts the 404.

triage.reason: There is no default scope or multi-tenancy gem in this codebase — scoping is done explicitly per query through scoped_invoices, which is why the one call that omits it is unscoped in fact.
Nothing narrows it: Invoice.find takes the raw parameter, and the only other constraint in the action is Integer() on the amount.
Invoice carries belongs_to :org (invoice.rb:2) and every other query filters on org_id, so the organisation is an explicit trust boundary in this model.

findings.title: Invoice update resolves the invoice with an unscoped find while every sibling action scopes it, allowing cross-organisation edits including the amount
findings.evidence: Four of the five actions in this controller use the scope: index (line 7), show (line 16), create (line 21) and void (line 44) all go through scoped_invoices. update alone calls Invoice.find(params[:id]) at line 34. The permitted attributes at lines 52-54 include amount_cents and currency alongside reference and memo, so the write is not limited to the typo fixes the comment at lines 31-32 describes.
findings.impact: A partner rewrites any invoice in the system by id: amount_cents, currency, reference, issued_on and posted_at, across organisations. The model validations still run — so the amount must stay a positive integer in an allowed currency — but nothing constrains whose invoice it is. Combined with the void action, which is correctly scoped, this is a straightforward path to altering another organisation's receivables.
findings.recommendation: Change line 34 to scoped_invoices.find(params[:id]). If partners really only need to fix a reference and a memo, narrow invoice_params for the update action so amount_cents and currency are not assignable after issue.

triage.reason: No policy object, no default scope and no before_action verifies ownership; the four sibling actions establish that the scope is the mechanism this codebase uses and that this line skips it.
The asymmetry is inside one file and one class: the same resource, four scoped reads and writes and one unscoped write.
issuer_belongs_to_org (invoice.rb:31) narrows nothing here — it validates the issuing user against the record's own org_id, which the update does not change.

findings.title: The export endpoint interpolates the caller's sort parameter into an ORDER BY clause wrapped in Arel.sql, which is SQL injection
findings.evidence: column = params[:sort].presence || "issued_on" (line 16) and the value goes straight into .order(Arel.sql("#{column} #{direction}")) at line 19. Arel.sql is the explicit opt-out from Rails' ORDER BY sanitisation — without it, Rails would raise UnknownAttributeReference on a non-column value. There is no allowlist: the only sanitiser in the file, safe_filename (line 48), is applied to params[:name] for the download filename and never to sort. coerce_pagination in the parent controller touches only limit and offset (application_controller.rb:41-42). direction is safely constrained at line 15; column is not.
findings.impact: ORDER BY is a position PostgreSQL evaluates per row, so an injected scalar subquery gives blind read access to any table the application role can reach — `?sort=(select case when (select count(*) from users where admin) > 0 then reference else memo end)` and its variants extract data one predicate at a time. The organisation scope on the rows being ordered does not constrain what the injected subquery reads.
findings.recommendation: Map the parameter to a literal through an allowlist before it reaches the query — `column = %w[issued_on amount_cents reference status].include?(params[:sort]) ? params[:sort] : "issued_on"` — and keep Arel.sql only around the resulting literal. The pack is explicit that an allowlist is the only valid control for the parts of a statement that cannot be bound.

triage.reason: params[:sort] is a request parameter and reaches line 19 unmodified; .presence only substitutes the default for blank, it does not constrain the value.
The framework control that would have caught this is exactly the one Arel.sql disables. Rack::Attack throttles the route (rack_attack.rb:21) but does not inspect parameters.
The sink is the ORDER BY of a live query executed by ActiveRecord; the string is parsed as SQL, not treated as data.

findings.title: Export listing and re-download expose every organisation's export files with no ownership check
findings.evidence: index (line 9) returns Dir.children(EXPORT_ROOT).sort — every filename in tmp/exports, with no filter and no relation to current_user.org_id. stream (line 29) resolves EXPORT_ROOT.join("#{params[:path]}.csv"), checks only File.exist? and sends the file. Neither action consults current_user, and there is no manifest table, no naming convention tying a file to an organisation, and no per-org subdirectory: create (line 22) hands the CSV back through send_data with a caller-chosen filename (line 23), so the names in that directory are partly attacker-chosen too.
findings.impact: A partner calls the list endpoint, reads the filenames of every other organisation's ledger export, and downloads each one. The CSV content is the invoice ledger — reference, memo, amount_cents, currency, status and issued_on (line 37) — so this is a complete cross-tenant disclosure of financial records with two ordinary API calls and no guessing.
findings.recommendation: Record exports in a table with an org_id and serve them by id through a scope, the way invoices are served: `current_user.org.exports.find(params[:id])`. Failing that, write each export under a per-organisation directory derived from the session, never from the request, and filter the listing by the caller's organisation.

triage.reason: The only filters on these actions are authenticate_partner! and coerce_pagination; nothing between them and the filesystem consults the organisation.
The files are ledger exports of a specific organisation's invoices — the same rows the invoices endpoint scopes carefully by org_id.
The route constraint at config/routes.rb:18 narrows the character set of the name, which stops traversal, but it does not narrow which of the existing files may be fetched.

findings.title: A CSV import row can name any organisation, so a partner writes invoices into another organisation's ledger
findings.class: Mass assignment across a tenant boundary
findings.evidence: org_id: row["org_id"].presence || upload.org_id — the uploader's own organisation is used only as a fallback when the CSV column is blank. Every other field in build_row is taken from the row as well, and the rows are written with Invoice.insert_all (line 19). Nothing compares row["org_id"] against upload.org_id, and nothing rejects a row whose org_id differs. The upload's own organisation is available on the very same line, which is what makes the precedence order the defect.
findings.impact: A partner uploads a CSV whose org_id column names another organisation and injects invoices into that organisation's ledger — arbitrary references, memos and amounts, appearing as genuine receivables. At the batch sizes the file is written for (2,000 rows per statement, a 40k-line file in the comment at lines 6-8) this is bulk falsification, and because insert_all bypasses the model there is no validation trail behind it.
findings.recommendation: Set org_id from upload.org_id unconditionally and ignore the column, or reject the whole upload when any row names a different organisation. The tenant of an import is a property of the upload, never of its contents.

triage.reason: row["org_id"] is a cell in a caller-supplied CSV — upload.body — with no allowlist, cast or comparison between the parse at line 17 and the insert at line 19.
org_id is the tenant discriminator this entire application authorizes on: scoped_invoices filters on it and Invoice declares belongs_to :org.
insert_all issues a direct INSERT, so no model callback, validation or default could re-derive org_id from the upload — see the companion finding on the same file.

findings.title: The bulk import writes invoices with insert_all, which bypasses every validation and callback the model declares
findings.class: Validation gate enforced by one writer and not its sibling
findings.evidence: InvoicesController#create writes through scoped_invoices.new(...).save (lines 21-24), which runs the whole Invoice contract: reference presence and per-org uniqueness, amount_cents numericality greater_than 0, currency inclusion in USD/EUR/GBP/CAD, status inclusion in the four states, issuer_belongs_to_org, and the before_validation and before_save callbacks (invoice.rb:8-15). BulkImportJob writes the same table with Invoice.insert_all, which by design issues a raw multi-row INSERT and runs none of them. build_row makes the gap concrete: amount_cents is row["amount_cents"].to_i, which turns any non-numeric string into 0 and accepts a negative; currency and status are taken as given with only a fallback for blank; and posted_at, which stamp_posted_at exists to take away from the caller, is simply never set.
findings.impact: An imported ledger can hold invoices with zero or negative amounts, a currency outside the four supported, a status outside the four states, duplicate references within an organisation, and a ledger row that does not agree with its postings — every invariant the model file is written to hold. balance_cents (invoice.rb:19) and the month-end trial balance the assert_ledger_balanced comment describes are computed over rows that never passed the assertion.
findings.recommendation: Validate each row before the batch — build the Invoice objects, collect invoice.valid? failures into the upload's error field, and insert only the survivors — or move the invariants into database constraints (a CHECK on amount_cents, an enum or CHECK on currency and status, a unique index on (org_id, reference)) so a bulk path cannot get around them.

triage.reason: No database constraint is visible in the tree — there is no schema, migration or structure file — so nothing behind ActiveRecord re-imposes the model's rules. That absence is why the recommendation names constraints explicitly.
Both writers create rows in the same invoices table with the same columns; one runs the validation contract and the other does not, which is the WEB-24 test.
Every value written comes from the uploaded CSV; the only transformation is .to_s.strip on two strings and .to_i on the amount, none of which constrains the domain.

findings.title: The credential exchange endpoints are the only unauthenticated routes and the only ones the throttle configuration does not cover
findings.evidence: Three throttles are declared and each is keyed on a path prefix: /api/v1/invoices (line 18), /api/v1/exports (line 23) and /api/v1/admin (line 26). The token routes are /api/v1/tokens and /api/v1/tokens/refresh (config/routes.rb:5-6) and match none of those prefixes. Those are precisely the two actions that skip authentication — TokensController line 4 declares skip_before_action :authenticate_partner!, only: %i[create refresh] — and they compare secrets: partner.authenticate_secret(params[:client_secret]) at line 11, and a raw refresh-token lookup at line 20. There is no lockout counter, no failed-attempt tracking and no delay anywhere in the controller.
findings.impact: Client secrets and refresh tokens can be attacked at full request rate from a single address while every authenticated route around them is shaped. A successful guess yields a 30-minute bearer token (line 12) and, through refresh, an indefinitely renewable one.
findings.recommendation: Add throttles for /api/v1/tokens keyed on both the address and the submitted client_id, at a much tighter limit than the data routes, and add an exponential backoff or lockout bound to the client_id rather than to the address so a distributed attempt is also constrained.

triage.reason: Rack::Attack is the only limiter in the tree and its rules are enumerated in this one file; no controller-level throttle_classes or before_action supplements them.

An upstream WAF or gateway might rate-limit the login path, but no such configuration was provided. Per triage.md this is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS. The finding remains confirmed because what is being reported is the asymmetry inside this file: three siblings covered, the credential route not.
The blocklist at line 30 narrows nothing relevant — it matches three scanner user-agent strings at the start of the header, which an attacker simply does not send.

findings.title: Adjustment amounts are unbounded and unsigned, and the credit is applied with update_columns, which skips the ledger-balance assertion
findings.class: Business-logic abuse / validation bypass on a money mutation
findings.evidence: The controller converts the amount with Integer(adjustment_params[:amount_cents]) (adjustments_controller.rb:22) — a type check, not a domain check: it accepts negatives and arbitrarily large magnitudes, and there is no comparison against the invoice's own amount. credit! then writes @invoice.update_columns(amount_cents: @invoice.amount_cents - amount_cents, updated_at: @invoice.updated_at) at lines 32-35. update_columns issues a direct UPDATE, so none of the Invoice validations run: amount_cents numericality greater_than 0 (invoice.rb:9) and the before_save assert_ledger_balanced (invoice.rb:15, :39) are both skipped. The comment at lines 26-28 says the intent was to avoid updated_at churn and an association reload, and the code preserves updated_at explicitly, so the audit feed the comment names does not observe the change either.
findings.impact: A negative adjustment increases an invoice's amount; a credit larger than the invoice drives amount_cents to zero or below, which the model forbids and this path permits. The invoice and its LedgerEntry rows can be left disagreeing, which is the exact condition assert_ledger_balanced exists to prevent, and the deliberate updated_at freeze means the change does not surface to the audit subscribers.
findings.recommendation: Validate the amount in the controller — positive, integer, and not greater than the invoice's outstanding balance — and apply the credit with update! (or an atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE amount_cents >= :amount`) so the model contract runs and a concurrent double-credit cannot drive the balance negative. If the audit feed must not fire, suppress it explicitly rather than by freezing a timestamp.

triage.reason: The validations are the compensating control and update_columns is the construct that bypasses them; the Adjustment.create! on the line above validates the Adjustment row, not the Invoice.
amount_cents comes from the request body through permitted parameters (adjustments_controller.rb:43); Integer() constrains the type and nothing constrains the value.
Nothing narrows the write: update_columns issues the UPDATE on the invoice resolved by the caller's own parameter, with no predicate on the current amount and no bound on the delta.

findings.title: The CSV export writes cell values unmodified, so a memo beginning with a formula character executes when the file is opened in a spreadsheet
findings.evidence: to_csv maps each header to invoice.public_send(h) and appends the raw value (line 42). Two of the six exported columns are partner-writable free text: reference and memo are both in invoice_params (invoices_controller.rb:53) and both flow into the CSV. Nothing prefixes, quotes defensively or strips the leading =, +, -, @, tab or carriage-return characters that Excel, LibreOffice and Google Sheets treat as the start of a formula. The response is sent as text/csv (line 24) with a caller-influenced filename.
findings.impact: A partner sets a memo to a formula and the finance team, who the comment at lines 12-13 says open these exports in a spreadsheet template, executes it on open — typically a DDE or HYPERLINK payload that exfiltrates neighbouring cells or prompts for a download. The attacker chooses the content and a different organisation's staff open it, so the boundary is real even though the vulnerability fires outside the application.
findings.recommendation: Prefix any cell whose first character is one of = + - @ (or a tab or carriage return) with a single quote, or wrap the value so the spreadsheet reads it as text, and apply it in to_csv so every exporter inherits it.

triage.reason: memo and reference are permitted attributes written directly by partners through both the create and update actions, and the bulk import writes them too.
The sink is a .csv file served for download and, per the file's own comment, opened in a spreadsheet template — the context in which a leading = is executable rather than textual.
There is no other layer neutralising the value: this is the only place the export is assembled.

findings.title: Settlement silently falls back to the acquirer sandbox when ACQUIRER_BASE_URL is unset, marking invoices paid against canned fixtures
findings.evidence: base = ENV.fetch("ACQUIRER_BASE_URL", SANDBOX_BASE_URL) supplies the sandbox as the fallback, and the next line selects the compiled-in SANDBOX_API_KEY whenever base equals it — so an unset variable produces a fully functional client pointed at the sandbox, with no error and no log line. ENV.fetch is used without a default for ACQUIRER_API_KEY on the same line, which shows the author knew how to make a missing variable fail loudly and chose not to for the base URL. SANDBOX_API_KEY is a literal at line 9.
findings.impact: If a deployment is missing ACQUIRER_BASE_URL, settle! (line 38) captures against the sandbox, which the comment at line 8 says only ever answers with canned fixtures — response.captured? returns true and the invoice is marked paid and stamped settled_at (line 42) without any real capture. The failure is silent and financial. The hardcoded key itself is a documented public sandbox value and carries little independent risk.
findings.recommendation: Require ACQUIRER_BASE_URL with ENV.fetch and no default, so a missing variable aborts at boot; keep the sandbox selectable only through an explicit value. Move the sandbox key to configuration alongside the live one so no credential is compiled in.

triage.reason: settle! has zero callers anywhere in the tree, so I cannot show that the sandbox client is reached by any shipped path; the caller may live in a file outside the scope I was given. Per triage.md that is UNKNOWN and caps this at probable — which is also why the severity is low rather than higher.

The defect reported is the silent configuration fallback at line 49, not the constant on line 9. For the constant alone FP-02 would be the deciding rule and would exculpate it - it is the acquirer's published sandbox value, shared by every integrator and reachable only on the sandbox host - so it is recorded as evidence of the fallback rather than as a leaked secret.
There is no other layer that would catch the misconfiguration: nothing asserts at boot which acquirer the process is pointed at.

findings.title: The label download joins a caller-controlled tail path onto the label root with no canonicalisation, giving arbitrary file read
findings.evidence: The route is #[get("/labels/{shipment_id}/{label_ref:.*}")] (line 22) — the .* tail matches separators, so label_ref is a multi-segment, percent-decoded string. Line 39 is state.cfg.label_root.join(&label_ref) followed by fs::read at line 40. Nothing normalises it: there is no canonicalize, no starts_with check against label_root, no rejection of .. and no rejection of a leading separator. Rust's PathBuf::join replaces the base entirely when the argument is absolute, so /api/v1/labels/<uuid>//etc/passwd reads /etc/passwd, and ../ sequences escape the root the ordinary way. The only sanitiser in the file, download_name (line 13), is applied solely to the Content-Disposition filename at line 46 — it never touches the path used to open the file. actix registers no path-normalising middleware in main.rs.
findings.impact: Any caller holding an API key and one shipment of their own reads any file the process can open: the environment-derived database URL, container secrets, the binary itself, other tenants' label PDFs. The ownership check at lines 30-37 gates that the caller owns some shipment, not which file they then receive.
findings.recommendation: Reject label_ref if it contains a separator, a .. component or is absolute; then resolve with fs::canonicalize and assert the result starts_with the canonicalised label_root before opening. Better, store labels under a server-generated identifier and look the filename up from the shipment record rather than accepting it from the path.

triage.reason: The tree contains no path-normalising middleware — main.rs registers only Logger and AuthGuard — and actix does not normalise tail-match parameters. The equivalent control in fleet-relay (CanonicalPath) has no counterpart here.
label_ref is a route parameter, decoded by actix and used verbatim. download_name transforms a copy for the header, not the value passed to join.
The shipment ownership check narrows who may call the handler; it does not narrow which path the handler then reads, because shipment_id and label_ref are independent parameters.

findings.title: Bulk import stages attachments at a path taken from the request body, which is an arbitrary file write
findings.evidence: bulk_import iterates the posted rows and calls stage_attachment(&state.cfg.import_root, name, row.attachment_body.as_bytes()) at line 65, where name is row.attachment_name straight out of the JSON body (line 25). stage_attachment does root.join(name) at line 75, creates every missing parent directory with fs::create_dir_all (line 78) and writes the bytes with fs::write (line 81). There is no sanitisation, no component check, no absolute-path rejection and no canonicalisation anywhere on that path; the file contents are attacker-supplied too (attachment_body, line 27).
findings.impact: An authenticated shipper writes a file of chosen content to any path the process can write, and create_dir_all means the target directory need not already exist. That reaches the service's own configuration and binaries, a cron or systemd drop-in directory if the process is privileged, an SSH authorized_keys file, or anything a co-located component reads — which is remote code execution in most deployments. The batch limit at line 39 bounds the row count, not the paths.
findings.recommendation: Derive the stored filename on the server — a UUID, or a hash of the content — and keep the caller's name only as metadata. If the caller's name must be used, strip it to a single path component, reject .. and absolute paths, canonicalise and assert containment under import_root before writing.

triage.reason: The only checks in bulk_import are the AuthGuard middleware, which establishes an account, and the batch-size test at line 39. Neither constrains the path.
attachment_name is an Option<String> deserialised from the request body with serde and passed through without inspection.
The writer is a remote shipper authenticated with an API key; the filesystem being written is the service's, which is a different trust domain.

findings.title: Webhook subscription update takes the subscription id from the path and checks no ownership, so any account rewrites any other account's callback URL
findings.evidence: create_subscription checks ownership explicitly: if body.account_id != principal.account_id it returns 403 (lines 26-28). update_subscription does not compare the principal to anything — it takes web::Path<i64> at line 47 and calls store.update_subscription(id, &body.callback_url, &body.events) at line 56, whose statement is `update webhook_subscriptions set callback_url = $2, events = $3 ... where id = $1` (store.rs:165) with no account_id predicate. The principal is used only to write a log line at line 60, which is the clearest evidence that the value was available and simply not used as a filter. The ids are sequential i64 primary keys, so they need no guessing.
findings.impact: Any account holder iterates subscription ids and points every other account's webhook at a server they control, which redirects the scan-event stream — shipment references, states and timing for other shippers — to the attacker, and simultaneously denies the victim their own notifications. The SSRF validator on line 52 still runs, so the destination must be an external https host, which is exactly what an attacker wants.
findings.recommendation: Add `and account_id = $n` to the update statement and pass principal.account_id, then return 404 when rows_affected is zero. The same pattern is already correct one function above.

triage.reason: AuthGuard establishes which account is calling but performs no per-object authorization; the store method carries no scope; and there is no policy layer between them.
The two handlers in this file reach the same effect on the same table, and one carries the ownership gate while the other does not — decidable by reading two functions side by side.
validate_callback_url narrows the destination to an external https host but places no constraint at all on whose subscription is being rewritten.

findings.title: The bulk import stores each row's callback URL without the SSRF validation the single-shipment endpoint applies
findings.class: Validation gate enforced by one writer and not its sibling
findings.evidence: shipments::create validates before it writes: `if let Some(callback) = body.callback_url.as_deref() { validate_callback_url(callback)?; }` at lines 79-81, and only then calls insert_shipment. bulk_import declares the same field on BulkRow (imports.rs:23) and copies it into NewShipment at line 52 with no call to validate_callback_url anywhere in the file — the import module does not even reference the function, while webhooks.rs imports it for both of its handlers. Both writers land in the same shipments.callback_url column: insert_shipment binds it at store.rs:62 and insert_shipments_bulk at store.rs:81.
findings.impact: The egress filter is a one-line detour away.
