A shipper posts a manifest whose rows carry callback URLs pointing at loopback, the cluster's internal DNS names or a link-local metadata address, and the component that later fires those callbacks makes the request from inside the delivery VPC — which shipments.rs:32-33 states is precisely the position the validator exists to protect. Twenty thousand rows per call means the bypass is also a scanning primitive.
findings.recommendation: Call validate_callback_url on every row before the batch is built, and reject the whole request on the first failure. Better, move the validation into the store layer or behind a newtype so a URL cannot reach the column without having passed it.

triage.reason: The two writers reach the same effect — a shipments row whose callback_url will be dialled — and one runs the validator while the other does not. That is the WEB-24 test and it is decidable across two files in the same crate.

The component that actually dials callback_url is not in this crate: Cargo.toml declares no HTTP client, and no egress policy or network manifest was provided. So I cannot show the request is made, nor that a proxy constrains it. Per triage.md this is UNKNOWN and caps the finding at probable.
row.callback_url is deserialised from the request body and copied at line 52 with no inspection.

findings.title: The SSRF validator inspects only the literal host string, so a hostname that resolves inward and several internal address forms pass
findings.evidence: The function requires https (line 37) and then filters on the host as written: three literal suffix and equality tests at line 45, and — only when host_str itself parses as an IP address (line 49) — a range test. Nothing resolves the name, so any hostname whose A or AAAA record points at an internal address passes untouched, and the resolution that happens later at connect time is never compared to what was validated. The IPv6 arm at line 52 covers only is_loopback and is_unspecified: unique-local fc00::/7 is not covered, and an IPv4-mapped address such as ::ffff:169.254.169.254 is neither loopback nor unspecified, so it passes although its embedded IPv4 is link-local. The IPv4 arm omits 0.0.0.0/8 and the 100.64.0.0/10 carrier range. There is no redirect policy, because the dialling code is not here.
findings.impact: A subscriber points a callback at a name they control that resolves to 169.254.169.254 or to an in-cluster service and reaches it from inside the delivery VPC — cloud instance credentials, unauthenticated internal APIs, the OPA-style sidecars such deployments carry. The same hostname can answer differently on a second lookup, so even a validator that did resolve would need to pin the address it validated.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the hostname at validation time, check every returned address against a deny list that includes loopback, private, link-local, unique-local, IPv4-mapped and unspecified ranges, and then connect to the address you checked rather than re-resolving. Disable redirect following in the dialling client, or re-run the check on each hop. An allowlist of subscriber domains is stronger still.

triage.reason: This function is the egress control; there is no proxy configuration, network policy or allowlist elsewhere in the crate.

A network-layer egress restriction in the delivery VPC would bound this, and no such artifact was provided. UNKNOWN per triage.md, which caps the finding at probable — as does the absence of the dialling client from this crate.
The URL is the caller's, from the shipment payload and the subscription payload; the checks constrain its shape, not its origin.

findings.title: The unauthenticated tracking endpoint returns the full shipment record including the recipient's name, address and phone number
findings.class: Excessive data exposure on an unauthenticated endpoint
findings.evidence: AuthGuard exempts this route through a suffix test — is_open_endpoint returns true for any path ending "/status" (auth.rs:24) — so the handler runs with no principal. It calls store.get_shipment_any_account(id) (line 135), whose statement selects SHIPMENT_COLUMNS with no account predicate (store.rs:107), and serialises the result as ShipmentView, which declares recipient_name, recipient_address and recipient_phone alongside id, reference, state and last_scan_at (lines 21-30). The same struct is what the authenticated get_one returns, so the unauthenticated caller receives exactly as much as the account owner. The route is not the only path matching the exemption: /api/v1/labels/{uuid}/anything/status also ends in "/status" and so skips the guard, although its handler then fails on the missing Principal extractor rather than serving anything.
findings.impact: The shipment UUID is the only credential, and it travels in an SMS link — forwarded, screenshotted, stored in message backups and often logged by URL scanners and link previewers. Anyone who obtains one reads a named individual's full delivery address and phone number, which is personal data well beyond the tracking state the page needs.
findings.recommendation: Return a narrow view from this endpoint — state, last_scan_at and at most a masked reference — rather than the struct the authenticated endpoint uses. Replace the suffix test in is_open_endpoint with an exact route match, and consider a short-lived signed tracking token in place of the raw UUID.

triage.reason: A named recipient's postal address and telephone number are personal data by any reading; nothing in the tree marks these columns as synthetic or public.

The intended exposure, per the comment at lines 20-22, is a tracking page for the recipient. That justifies exposing the state, and it does not justify exposing the whole record — the finding moves to the field list rather than disappearing.
The UUID narrows who can guess a given shipment but not what is returned once one is known, and the suffix match makes the exemption wider than the single route it was written for.

findings.title: The carrier callback compares the HMAC signature with a plain string inequality and accepts any replay of a valid one
findings.evidence: The expected digest is computed correctly with hmac and sha2 (lines 87-90), and then compared with `if provided != expected` (line 92) — Rust's str inequality short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the comparison time varies with the length of the matching prefix. The hmac crate supplies Mac::verify_slice for exactly this and it is not used, and Cargo.toml declares neither subtle nor constant_time_eq. Separately, the signature covers only the body (mac.update(&body), line 89): there is no timestamp, nonce or sequence number in the signed material and no store of seen signatures, so a captured request stays valid indefinitely.
findings.impact: This comparison is the only authentication on the route — main.rs:42 registers carrier_callback outside the guarded scope precisely because the HMAC is meant to be the credential. A forged signature would let an attacker drive apply_scans (store.rs:186) and rewrite shipment states for that account. Remote timing recovery of an HMAC over a network is difficult, which is why the severity is low; the replay half needs no timing at all — anyone who observes one valid callback can resend it whenever they choose.
findings.recommendation: Replace lines 87-93 with mac.verify_slice(&hex::decode(provided)?), which compares in constant time and rejects a malformed hex signature. Include a timestamp header in the signed material, reject anything outside a few minutes, and record recently seen signatures to make replay ineffective.

triage.reason: There is no other check on this route: main.rs registers it outside the AuthGuard scope, and the handler's only rejection paths are an unknown account (line 79) and this comparison.
It is not defence in depth behind a working control — it is the control. The low severity reflects the difficulty of the timing attack, not a second layer catching it.
Both operands are hex strings of equal length in the success case, so the comparison genuinely walks byte by byte; there is no length short-circuit that would flatten the signal.

findings.title: The admin router is mounted with no session and no scope middleware, exposing session listing, revocation and org-wide sign-out to anyone
findings.class: Missing authentication and authorization on an administrative surface
findings.evidence: Line 46 attaches the guard to the profile router — profileRouter.use(requireSession) — and line 47 mounts it. Line 50 mounts adminRouter with no equivalent line anywhere: routes/admin.ts creates the router at line 10 and registers three handlers with no middleware, and grep over the tree shows requireScope (defined at middleware/require_session.ts:37) has zero callers — the scope control that SCOPES_BY_ROLE was written for, with its sessions:read and sessions:revoke entries at store.ts:48, is never applied to anything. The three handlers act immediately: listSessions on a query parameter (admin.ts:13-17), revokeSession on a path parameter (line 22) and purgeOrgSessions on a path parameter (line 27).
findings.impact: GET /admin/sessions?org=<id> returns, with no credential, every live Session object for that organisation — and Session carries id, userId, orgId, roles and scopes (store.ts:15-23). The id in that listing is the session identifier, which combines with the unsigned-legacy-cookie defect reported next into complete takeover of any listed account. DELETE /admin/sessions/:id signs any user out and POST /admin/orgs/:orgId/logout-everyone signs out an entire organisation, both unauthenticated, which is a denial of service on its own.
findings.recommendation: Apply adminRouter.use(requireSession) and adminRouter.use(requireScope("sessions:read")) before mounting, with requireScope("sessions:revoke") on the two destructive routes, and stop returning the session id from the listing — return an opaque handle the revoke endpoint can resolve. Add a test asserting every router mounted in buildApp has a guard.

triage.reason: The two middlewares registered globally are the CORS layer (line 11) and the allowed-host check (line 18); neither establishes identity. requireSession is applied to exactly one router and it is not this one.
The asymmetry is two adjacent lines in one function: line 46 guards the profile router, line 50 mounts the admin router bare.
Nothing binds /admin to a separate listener or interface: buildApp returns one Application and main listens on one port (line 56).

findings.title: A cookie that fails signature verification is accepted through an unsigned legacy format, so a session id alone authenticates
findings.evidence: const sessionId = (await verify(raw)) ?? decodeLegacy(raw). verify (cookie.ts:36) does the HMAC comparison properly; decodeLegacy (cookie.ts:53) splits the cookie on a pipe and returns parts[1] whenever there are exactly two parts and the second is non-empty — no key, no MAC, no check of any kind. The fallback fires on every cookie the signature rejects, so an attacker sets nw_sid=x|<session-id> and is authenticated as the owner of that session. The failure mode compounds: signingKeys() (config.ts:23) reads SESSION_SIGNING_KEYS with a default of the empty string, so with the variable unset the loop in verify iterates zero keys, returns null for every cookie, and routes all traffic to the unsigned path.
findings.impact: The cookie signature is not a control. Combined with the unauthenticated /admin/sessions listing reported above, which hands out live session ids, this is unauthenticated takeover of any account in any organisation: read the id, set the pipe cookie, and requireSession loads the real Session at line 27 and puts it on ctx.state. Even without that listing, the ids are guessable — see the next finding.
findings.recommendation: Delete decodeLegacy and the fallback; require a valid signature. If the desktop client genuinely still holds v1 cookies, force those users through a re-login instead of accepting an unauthenticated format, and make signingKeys() throw at start-up when the list is empty so a missing secret fails closed rather than opening this path for everyone.

triage.reason: loadSession (store.ts:88) at line 27 confirms the session exists but does not authenticate the bearer — existence is exactly what an attacker who supplies a real id relies on.

The fallback is unconditional in the shipped code path: no environment flag, build profile or version check gates it, and the comment at lines 18-20 describes it as current behaviour pending a release train.
The signature is not defence in depth here — it is the sole integrity control on the session cookie, and the fallback removes it.

findings.title: Session identifiers are generated from Math.random, so they are predictable from observed values
findings.evidence: newSessionId builds 32 hex characters one nibble at a time from Math.floor(Math.random() * 16) (lines 57-61). Math.random is a non-cryptographic PRNG — V8 seeds an xorshift128+ generator whose internal state is recoverable from a modest run of outputs, after which past and future values are computable. The id is used directly as the session key: mintSession stores the session at `session:${session.id}` (line 82) and requireSession loads it by that key. The comment at lines 51-55 justifies the choice on the grounds that ids only need uniqueness within the TTL and are re-signed before leaving the process — but the signature is bypassable through decodeLegacy, and uniqueness is not the property a session id needs. crypto.randomUUID is used elsewhere in the same codebase (routes/auth.ts:73), so the correct primitive was available.
findings.impact: An attacker who collects a run of ids — by logging in repeatedly, which mints one per call — recovers the generator state and predicts the ids issued to other users in the same window. With decodeLegacy accepting an unsigned cookie, a predicted id is immediately a working session. Even with signatures enforced, predictable ids undermine the revocation and listing model built on them.
findings.recommendation: Generate ids from the CSPRNG: crypto.getRandomValues over a 32-byte buffer rendered as hex, or crypto.randomUUID. Rotate every existing session, since ids minted by the current generator cannot be assumed unguessed.

triage.reason: The value is the session secret itself. WEB-03 names Math.random explicitly and the exculpation it offers — that the value governs no access decision — is false here: this value is the access decision.
The cookie signature would be the compensating layer, and it is bypassable through the legacy path in require_session.ts:21. It also fails independently when SESSION_SIGNING_KEYS is unset.
32 hex characters looks like 128 bits of entropy and is not: the generator supplies at most its own state, and the nibble-at-a-time construction exposes that state more readily, not less.

findings.title: The remember-me branch writes the session cookie inline and drops HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite, for thirty days
findings.evidence: setSessionCookie (cookie.ts:62) is documented at lines 58-61 as the single place that knows how a session cookie is shaped and sets httpOnly, secure, sameSite: "lax", path, domain and maxAge (lines 68-73). The remember branch bypasses it: ctx.cookies.set(SESSION_COOKIE, await sign(session.id), { path, domain, maxAge }) at lines 35-39 — three of the six options, and the three that are missing are exactly the security attributes. The comment at lines 32-34 explains the bypass as being about the lifetime alone, and setSessionCookie already takes a ttlSeconds parameter (cookie.ts:65) that would have covered it.
findings.impact: For every user who ticks 'keep me signed in', the session cookie is readable by any script on the origin, is transmitted over plain HTTP if the browser is ever induced to make one, and is attached to cross-site requests — which turns every state-changing endpoint into a CSRF target for thirty days. The cookie domain is the parent domain .northwind.test (config.ts:10), so any subdomain shares it.
findings.recommendation: Call setSessionCookie(ctx, session.id, config.rememberTtlSeconds) — the helper already accepts the longer window — and delete the inline set. Consider sameSite: "strict" for the long-lived variant.

triage.reason: Nothing rewrites Set-Cookie after the handler: buildApp registers CORS, a host check and a logger, none of which touches response cookies.
The comparison is inside one file against a helper in another: six options in the helper, three in the inline call, and the three omitted are the security ones.
This is not a development-only relaxation gated on an environment: the branch is selected by the request body's remember flag at line 31.

findings.title: The profile cache key is the subject's id alone, but the cached value is the view computed for whoever asked first, so contact details leak between viewers
findings.class: Authorization bypass through a shared cache key
findings.evidence: profileKey (store.ts:129) returns `profile:v2:${userId}` — keyed on the subject and nothing else. viewFor (line 24) computes a value that depends entirely on the viewer: self (line 31), supporting (lines 35-37) and the sessions:read scope (line 39) decide whether email, phone, mfaEnrolled and recoveryCodesLeft are attached. The handler reads that shared key first and returns the hit verbatim (lines 57-60), before viewFor ever runs, and on a miss writes the viewer-specific view back to the shared key (line 71) with a fifteen-minute TTL. The PATCH handler does the same at line 100, storing viewFor(session, updated) — the editor's view — under the same shared key.
findings.impact: When a user views their own profile, the privileged view is cached; for the next fifteen minutes every other authenticated caller requesting that profile receives it, including email, phone, MFA enrolment state and the number of remaining recovery codes. The support-engineer and operator branches poison the cache the same way. The three conditions in viewFor are the authorization control for this data and the cache serves the result around all of them.
findings.recommendation: Include the viewer's entitlement in the key — `profile:v3:${id}:${self ? "self" : supporting ? "support" : scope}` — or, more robustly, cache only the base ProfileRecord and run viewFor on every response so the decision is never memoised. Bump the version segment to abandon existing entries.

triage.reason: requireSession establishes who is calling but performs no field-level check; viewFor is the only control and the cache hit at line 58 returns before it is reached.
The leaked fields are email, phone, MFA enrolment and remaining recovery codes — personal data, and in the last two cases account-recovery intelligence.
The key is as wide as it reads. The narrowing conditions all live in viewFor, which the cache path skips entirely.

findings.title: Every ordinary member holds the profile:write scope, so the profile PATCH check admits any user to any profile in any organisation
findings.evidence: The gate is `if (session.userId !== id && !hasScope(session.scopes, "profile:write"))` — self, or the scope. SCOPES_BY_ROLE (store.ts:44-49) grants profile:write to member, the baseline role, as well as to admin, and mintSession assigns those scopes from the user's roles at line 69. So the second disjunct is satisfied for essentially every authenticated user, which makes the first disjunct decorative. There is no organisation comparison anywhere in the handler: unlike viewFor, which checks session.orgId === record.orgId for the support branch (line 37), the PATCH path never looks at orgId. The write at line 99 then stores the modified record under `directory:${id}` with a one-year TTL — overwriting the authoritative directory entry loadProfile reads (store.ts:143).
findings.impact: Any member edits any other user's displayName and phone, across organisations, and the change persists in the directory for a year. Changing a phone number is not cosmetic: it is the number an SMS-based recovery or verification flow would reach, and the same handler also writes the viewer's rendered view into the shared profile cache, compounding the leak reported above.
findings.recommendation: Split the scopes: keep profile:write as self-service and introduce a distinct profile:write:any for the administrative case, granted to admin only. Add an organisation check to the non-self branch, and stop writing the directory record from this handler — patch the system of record and let the cache refill.

triage.reason: requireSession is the only middleware on this router and it establishes identity, not object permission. No policy layer sits between the handler and writeCached.
This is the inverse of the FP-11 shape: the check reads as a narrow self-or-privileged gate and in fact admits everyone, because the scope it tests for is in the baseline role's grant list.
orgId is a first-class boundary in this service — listSessions, purgeOrgSessions and the supporting branch of viewFor all key on it — and this handler crosses it.

findings.title: The post-authentication continue endpoint redirects to any URL supplied in a query parameter
findings.evidence: const next = ctx.request.url.searchParams.get("next") ?? "/dashboard" (line 60) and ctx.response.redirect(next) (line 61). There is no check that the value is relative, no allowlist of destinations, no comparison against config.allowedHosts and no rejection of a scheme. The route sits on authRouter, which main.ts:43 mounts ahead of any session middleware, so it is reachable unauthenticated; the comment at lines 57-58 states it is the landing point the identity provider bounces the browser back to.
findings.impact: A phishing link of the form https://accounts.northwind.test/auth/continue?next=https://attacker.example carries the legitimate, recognisable hostname through the mail filter and the user's own inspection, and lands the victim on the attacker's page immediately after they have signed in — the moment they are most primed to re-enter credentials. Because this is the identity provider's return endpoint, the destination is also where an implementation that appended a token to the return URL would deliver it.
findings.recommendation: Accept only same-origin destinations: reject anything that does not begin with a single forward slash (rejecting // and /\ as well), or resolve the value against the service origin and confirm the resulting host is in config.allowedHosts. Keep /dashboard as the fallback for anything rejected.

triage.reason: next is read straight from the query string with no validation between line 60 and line 61.
The host-allowlist middleware at main.ts:18 validates the inbound Host header of this request; it says nothing about the outbound Location the handler writes.
No other layer constrains the redirect target — there is no CSP frame-ancestors or navigation policy in the tree — so nothing reduces the impact to informational.

findings.title: The password reset link is built from the raw Host header while the host guard compares only the portion before the colon
findings.class: Host header injection / password reset poisoning
findings.evidence: The guard at main.ts:19 computes `(ctx.request.headers.get("host") ?? "").split(":")[0]` and requires the result to be in config.allowedHosts. The reset handler at line 74 reads the same header without that transformation — `ctx.request.headers.get("host") ?? config.allowedHosts[0]` — and interpolates the whole value into the link at line 75. The two readings of one header differ, which is the defect: a header of the form `accounts.northwind.test:@evil.example` satisfies the guard, because everything before the first colon is the allowed host, while the link becomes https://accounts.northwind.test:@evil.example/auth/reset/confirm?token=..., where the portion before the @ is parsed as userinfo and the authority is evil.example. queueResetEmail logs only new URL(link).pathname (line 81), so the substitution leaves no trace in the log.
findings.impact: The reset mail delivered to a real user carries a link whose host is the attacker's, with a valid single-use reset token in the query string. Clicking it hands the token over and the account is taken over without the attacker ever needing the victim's mailbox.
findings.recommendation: Never build a link from a request header. Construct the reset URL from a configured canonical origin — config.allowedHosts[0] is already the fallback on that very line and should be the only source. If a per-tenant host is genuinely needed, look it up from configuration keyed on the validated host, and make the guard and the consumer read the header through one shared parser.

triage.reason: The guard at main.ts:21 is the candidate compensating control and it inspects a different string than the sink does — split(":")[0] versus the full header — so it does not constrain the value that reaches line 75.

Whether Deno's HTTP server accepts a Host header containing @ and forwards it to the handler could not be established: no runtime is available here and the behaviour is not documented in the tree. If it rejects such a header the finding collapses, which is why this is probable and not confirmed — the fix is the same either way, since the guard and the sink parsing one header differently is a defect regardless.
The Host header is caller-supplied. The guard constrains its prefix, not the whole value the sink consumes.

findings.title: Neither the login endpoint nor the password reset endpoint is rate limited, and no limiter exists anywhere in the service
findings.evidence: buildApp (main.ts:8-53) registers four middlewares — CORS, the host check, the request logger and requireSession on the profile router — and no limiter. There is no rate-limiting dependency in deps.ts, which imports oak, cors and redis only. The login handler compares credentials at line 23 and returns 401 on failure with no counter incremented, no delay and no lockout: nothing in mintSession, findUserByEmail or verifyPassword records an attempt. The reset endpoint at line 64 is likewise unbounded, and it triggers an outbound email per call.
findings.impact: Passwords can be attacked at full request rate against a known email address, and the directory can be sprayed with a single common password across many addresses. verifyPassword uses PBKDF2-SHA256 at 210,000 iterations (store.ts:170), which is a sound cost for the defender and also makes the endpoint an amplification target: each attempt costs the server far more than the attacker. The unbounded reset endpoint is a mail-bombing primitive against any known address.
findings.recommendation: Add a limiter keyed on both the source address and the submitted email, with a progressive lockout on the identity rather than only on the address, and a separate tighter quota for /auth/reset. A Redis counter is a few lines given the client already in the process.

triage.reason: No limiter exists in the tree to compensate — deps.ts enumerates the entire dependency surface and contains none, and buildApp registers none.

An upstream gateway might throttle /auth, and no configuration for one was provided. Per triage.md that is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS. The finding stays confirmed because it reports the absence inside the service, which is fully established.

The reset endpoint's uniform response (lines 68-70) correctly prevents enumeration, which is a different control; it does nothing about attempt volume, so no working layer reduces this to informational.
